title: Ninety-five theses (1517)
hook: Luther posts theses for debate, and printers carry them across Europe

segments.voice: Yesterday, Romans one seventeen: the just shall live by faith, and a frightened monk who felt the gates open. Your line was the gates opened. What were you given that you didn't earn? Day eight hundred fifty-three.

Hammer, nail, church door. That's the picture on posters, in films, on coffee mugs: a monk in a black habit nailing a sheet of paper to a wooden door while a crowd gasps. The story goes that Martin Luther did exactly that, at the castle church in Wittenberg, on the eve of All Saints. Historians still argue about the hammer. What isn't in doubt is the paper. It was written in Latin, in numbered points, and its title called it a disputation. In other words, it was an invitation to argue. Today: the ninety-five theses.

A thesis, in a university then, was a statement put up for debate. Scholars would post a list, and anyone could come and argue the other side. So Luther's theses were not a manifesto. They were questions, sharpened into claims, about the indulgence preaching we met two days ago. Luther preached in his town as well as teaching, and people from that town were coming back with indulgence letters and asking whether they still needed to change their lives. That bothered him. So the very first thesis goes straight to the words Jesus begins preaching with in Matthew. In the King James Bible: "Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." When Jesus said repent, Luther writes, he meant the whole life of a believer to be repentance. Not one payment. A whole life of turning. Further down, the questions get sharper. Near the end, Luther passes on questions he says ordinary people were asking. One goes, roughly: why does the pope, who is very rich, not build his great church in Rome with his own money instead of the money of poor believers? And here's the surprise. The theses don't yet throw out indulgences. They ask what indulgences can and can't do, and they say ordinary people deserve honest answers. Luther also sent them, with a letter, to his archbishop. Then something happened that he hadn't planned. Printers got hold of them, translated them out of Latin, and they ran across Germany and beyond far faster than any debate could be arranged. A list meant for scholars became a conversation for everyone. Christians have argued ever since about what that conversation broke and what it opened. But it began as a question.

Here's the practice: write one honest question down. Settle, and breathe. Let a question come up that you've been carrying but not asking. About faith, about work, about someone you love, about yourself. Not an accusation. A real question you'd like an honest answer to. When it comes, find a scrap of paper or your phone and write it down in one sentence. Then sit with it written there, outside your head. You don't have to post it anywhere. If you pray, you can bring the question to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Ninety-five theses. Luther's numbered claims for debate about indulgences, written in Latin for scholars, and carried by printers to everyone.
Your line: a question for debate. Today, ask your honest question of one person you trust, and then listen to their side all the way through. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Lutheran and other Protestant churches mark Reformation Day at the end of October, remembering the theses; in recent years some Catholic and Lutheran churches have marked it together.

fork.setup: you're Luther. people in your town think a paper letter means they no longer need to change their lives. what do you do?
options: keep quiet; it's above your rank.
write your questions down and invite a debate.
start a new church that week.
fork.reveal: he wrote numbered theses for debate and sent them to his archbishop. printers did the rest.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monk nails a list of complaints to a door.
what it means: numbered claims, in Latin, inviting scholars to debate what indulgences can and can't do.
what a scholar hears: an academic disputation that printers turned into a public conversation; the hammer itself is still argued over.

notes: Claims rule: the date (31 October 1517) is not stated in the voice; 'on the eve of All Saints' is given inside 'the story goes'. The posting itself is presented as disputed ('historians still argue about the hammer'): the account comes from Melanchthon after Luther's death. Confirm framing. The hook field is reworded from the index.
Thesis 1 and thesis 86 paraphrased. Confirm the paraphrase of 86 (why the pope, whose wealth exceeds the richest, does not build St. Peter's with his own money).
'The theses don't yet throw out indulgences' (cf. thesis 71); confirm.
'People from his own town were coming back with indulgence letters' refers to Wittenberg parishioners who bought from Tetzel across the border; general history, confirm.
Printing and translation into German and spread 'across Germany and beyond' is general history from the index hook; no time or count given.

Editor pass: 'Jesus's first sermon' (a claim Matthew does not make) changed to 'the words Jesus begins preaching with in Matthew'; 'parish priest' (inexact for an Augustinian friar who preached in the town church) changed to 'preached in his town'.
howItsDone: Reformation Day observance and joint Catholic-Lutheran commemorations (e.g. Lund) are general knowledge; confirm or trim.
Second editor: thesis 86 is now framed as Luther does, one of the sharp questions he says lay people were asking (theses 81 to 90), not as his own charge against the pope.
